995.title: Everywhere
995.hook: Jewish communities in Argentina, Canada, Australia, South Africa and beyond
995.howItsDone: Jewish communities around the world keep the same Shabbat and holidays in their own languages and accents, and in some synagogues a prayer for the welfare of the country is said during the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Triangle fire, and your line: remember the workers. A fire that rewrote the rules. A new week begins, and the map opens wide.

Friday evening reaches Melbourne while much of the world is still at work. Candles are lit, a blessing is sung over wine, and Shabbat begins. Hours later the sun sets over Cape Town, and it happens again. Then Buenos Aires. Then Toronto. As the evening rolls around the globe, the same small table scene keeps lighting up, city after city, in English, Spanish and Hebrew, in every kind of accent. Today, that whole moving line of candles. Today's word is Everywhere.
screen: `FRIDAY EVENING IN MELBOURNE.` → `THEN CAPE TOWN, BUENOS AIRES, TORONTO.` → `A LINE OF CANDLES AROUND THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The great wave didn't only flow to New York. Families leaving Eastern Europe looked for any door that would open. In Argentina, some settled in Jewish farming colonies out on the plains, and their riders came to be called Jewish gauchos. Others settled in Buenos Aires. In Canada, families settled in Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg. In South Africa, Jews from Lithuania were among those who arrived, and built synagogues from Johannesburg to Cape Town. In Australia, Jewish communities grew in Melbourne and Sydney. And there are more: Mexico, Brazil, Britain, France, places this path has already visited and places it hasn't. How do you live in so many places at once and stay one people? A line from the Psalms, sung in the Hallel on festivals, gives one picture of it: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof the LORD'S name is to be praised." Read on a globe, that line is a chain of candles. When the sun goes down in one city, it is still up in the next, and the praise passes along. So Jewish communities became part of each place: speaking its language, cheering its teams, serving in its schools and hospitals. In some synagogues a prayer for the country and its leaders is said in the service, each place in its own words. And at the same time, the same Torah is read, the same Shabbat begins, the same holidays come round. Everywhere doesn't mean nowhere. It means rooted in each city, and passing the same evening along to all the others.

segments.voice: Choose one place from today, Buenos Aires, Toronto, Winnipeg, Melbourne or Cape Town, and hold it in mind: somewhere there, right now, people are cooking, studying, praying. Then turn to your own city, and wish both places peace, in your own words, or, if you pray, with the words you already know.
Everywhere. Jewish communities in Argentina, Canada, Australia, South Africa and beyond, each rooted in its own city, all keeping the same Shabbat. Today's word.
Your line: rooted in each city. One Shabbat, lit city by city. Until next time.

996.title: Henrietta Szold
996.hook: teacher of immigrants and founder of Hadassah
996.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema with its line about teaching the commandments to your children in morning and evening prayers, and Hadassah still runs medical, education and volunteer work today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Everywhere, and your line: rooted in each city. One Shabbat, passed around the world. Today is the last stop of this time in the Americas, with a woman whose whole life was one verb.

Evening in Baltimore. The workday is done, and a classroom fills up with adults: tailors, peddlers, factory hands, newly arrived, still in their work clothes, tired to the bone. They've come to learn English. At the front stands a young woman with chalk on her fingers, a rabbi's daughter who teaches by day as well. She hands out the books and starts with the alphabet. Her name is Henrietta Szold, and today she's the word.
screen: `EVENING IN BALTIMORE.` → `WORKERS COME TO LEARN.` → `A TEACHER WITH CHALK ON HER FINGERS.`

segments.voice: Henrietta Szold grew up in Baltimore, the daughter of a rabbi, and became a teacher. When refugees from the pogroms began arriving in her city, she helped start a night school for them, teaching English and the ways of a new country to people who worked all day. Then she taught in another way: with a pen. She worked for years as an editor at the Jewish Publication Society, preparing books for American Jewish readers, the same society whose English Bible this path quotes. Then a journey changed her direction. She traveled to the land of Israel, then under Ottoman rule, and saw sickness and poverty there, especially among mothers and children. She came home and, with a group of women, founded an organization to send nurses and build care. They named it Hadassah. In the book of Esther, the queen has two names: the text calls her "Hadassah, that is, Esther." Esther was the one who spoke up for her people when it counted. Late in life, Szold moved to the land of Israel herself, and in the dark years of Nazi Germany she helped lead the work of bringing Jewish children out to safety, and then making sure they were cared for and taught. Teaching runs through every chapter. The Torah puts it plainly, in the passage Jews say morning and evening: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." Szold took that verse wide. Immigrants were her children. Readers were her children. Rescued children were her children. Teach, in every room she entered.

segments.voice: Bring back one thing someone once taught you that you still use: how to tie a knot, a word in another language, a recipe. See the person who taught it, how patient they were, and hold them with thanks for a few breaths.
Henrietta Szold. The Baltimore teacher of immigrants who founded Hadassah and helped bring children to safety. Today's word.
Your line: teach. A whole life, lived out as one verb. Day nine hundred ninety-six.

997.title: Next year in Jerusalem
997.hook: long before any movement, Jewish prayer faced Jerusalem
997.howItsDone: Jews traditionally face toward Jerusalem when they say the Amidah, the standing prayer, and the words next year in Jerusalem close the Passover seder and the final service of Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Henrietta Szold, and your line: teach. Today a new stretch opens, with a line much older than the movement it will feed.

It's late on the first night of Passover. The matzah is crumbs, the glasses refilled again and again, and a child is asleep across two chairs. Then, at the very end of the Haggadah, the table says one line together, sometimes sung, sometimes shouted: next year in Jerusalem. The same words come back at the close of Yom Kippur, after a whole day of fasting, as the last long blast of the shofar fades. Two great nights of the Jewish year end in the same place. Not in the room. In a city.
screen: `THE LAST LINE OF THE SEDER.` → `THE CLOSE OF YOM KIPPUR.` → `ENDING IN A CITY.`

segments.voice: The line rests on something Jews do every day: they pray facing Jerusalem. The roots are in the Tanakh. When Solomon dedicates the Temple, in the First Book of Kings, he asks God to hear people even when they are far away, if they pray toward the land, the city and the house. In the Book of Daniel, Daniel in Babylon goes up to his room, where the windows open toward Jerusalem, and prays there. The Talmud turns this into circles, one inside the next. Someone praying outside the land of Israel turns toward the land. Someone in the land turns toward Jerusalem. Someone in Jerusalem turns toward the Temple. Someone in the Temple turns toward its innermost room. So a whole scattered people, from every direction, leans in toward one point. The psalm of the exiles puts it as a vow: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." So what does next year in Jerusalem mean? Jews hear it in more than one way. For some, it is a plain hope to stand in the city. For some, it waits for the days of the Messiah and a rebuilt Temple. For some, it is a picture of a world repaired. And at seders in Jerusalem itself, some people add a word: next year in Jerusalem rebuilt. Even there, the line points somewhere further. This longing came long before any political plan. In the days ahead, people answer it in very different ways.
screen: `PRAYER FACES JERUSALEM.` · `CIRCLES, ONE INSIDE THE NEXT.` · `IF I FORGET THEE, O JERUSALEM.` · `A HOPE HEARD MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `NEXT YEAR IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: If you know which way Jerusalem lies from where you are, turn your chair or your body that way; if not, take your best guess, since the Talmud's circles are about leaning in, not about a compass. If you pray, say the psalm's line quietly, if I forget thee, O Jerusalem; if you don't, just hold the idea of one place a people has kept facing.
Jerusalem. The city Jews turn to face in prayer from everywhere in the world, the place the seder and Yom Kippur both close toward. Today's word.
Your line: leaning toward one point. The longing is old, and the answers are about to multiply. See you tomorrow.

998.title: Pogroms (1881)
998.hook: waves of violence in Russia push Jews to emigrate and to new ideas
998.howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the dead with memorial prayers and by saying 'may their memory be a blessing'; some families keep the stories and photographs of the towns their ancestors left.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem, and your line: leaning toward one point. Today, a hard chapter that turned an old longing into new plans. Go gently with it.

A town nobody in the family has seen for generations. A grandmother's recipe that came from there, a grandfather's trade, a surname that changed at a border. Ask a Jewish family in America, or England, or Argentina, why they left that town, and sometimes the answer is one word, a word that came into English from Russian and stayed. Behind it are towns in the Russian Empire where crowds turned on the Jews who lived there: doors smashed, shops emptied, people hurt and killed.
screen: `A TOWN IN THE OLD COUNTRY.` → `WHY DID THEY LEAVE?` → `ONE WORD FROM RUSSIAN.`

segments.voice: A pogrom is an attack by a crowd on a Jewish community: houses, shops, synagogues and people. In the Russian Empire, waves of them broke out across many towns, and came back again and again over the years that followed. Laws pressed in at the same time, limiting where Jews could live and what they could do. One town's name became a byword: Kishinev. After the violence there, the Hebrew poet Hayim Nahman Bialik went to see it. His poem, In the City of Slaughter, is hard to read. He grieves for the dead. And he turns, angry, on the survivors who hid, and even on heaven, which went on shining as if nothing happened. It is not a comforting poem. What the history teaches next: people did not answer in one way. Some left, in great numbers, for America and other shores; that is the great wave you met a few days ago. Some formed groups called Lovers of Zion and began farming villages in the land of Israel. A physician named Leon Pinsker wrote a pamphlet arguing that Jews would not be safe until they had a home of their own. Some young people organized to defend their streets. Others joined movements that wanted to stay and win equal rights right where they were. Same violence, different answers: leaving, building, defending, organizing. The days ahead follow some of those roads. Today, remember that each of these waves fell on real people with names.
screen: `ATTACKS ON JEWISH COMMUNITIES.` · `KISHINEV AND BIALIK'S POEM.` · `LEAVE, BUILD, DEFEND, ORGANIZE.` · then, large: `REAL PEOPLE WITH NAMES.`

segments.voice: You don't need any image of the violence; call up an ordinary street instead, a bakery, a schoolroom, a doorway with a mezuzah, and let it stand for the families who lived in those towns, and for any of your own family who came from far away. If you pray, ask that their memory be a blessing; if you don't, just hold the street quietly, full of people.
Pogrom. An attack by a crowd on a Jewish community, a word that came into English from Russian after waves of them in the Russian Empire. Today's word.
Your line: real people with names. Every wave of this history fell on a street like that one. That's day nine hundred ninety-eight.

999.title: Dreyfus
999.hook: a Jewish officer falsely convicted in France, and a writer who would not stay quiet
999.howItsDone: Jewish teaching ties the pursuit of justice to the Torah's command, 'Justice, justice shalt thou follow', and the Dreyfus case is often taught as a lesson in standing up against a public falsehood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard word, pogrom, and your line: real people with names. Today the scene moves west, to Paris, where nobody expected a story like this.

A courtyard in Paris on a cold morning. Soldiers stand in a square. An officer is marched to the center, and in front of everyone the braid is torn from his uniform and his sword is broken. He calls out that he is innocent. Beyond the railings a crowd jeers, and some of the shouting is not about spies at all, but about Jews. The officer is Captain Alfred Dreyfus. He is Jewish, he is loyal, and he did not do it.
screen: `A SWORD BROKEN IN A COURTYARD.` → `I AM INNOCENT.` → `A CROWD SHOUTING ABOUT JEWS.`

segments.voice: France was proud of being the country of liberty, equality and fraternity, and its Jews were full citizens. Dreyfus was an officer on the army's general staff. Then a secret note turned up: someone was passing military information to Germany. Suspicion fell on Dreyfus, on thin evidence, and a military court convicted him of treason. He was shipped to a prison on Devil's Island, off South America. Later, evidence pointed to a different officer. The army protected that officer, and he was acquitted. That's when the novelist Émile Zola wrote an open letter to the president of France, printed on a newspaper's front page under two huge words: J'accuse. I accuse. He named the men he said had covered up the truth. Zola was tried, convicted, and left the country. France split, families and friends arguing at dinner tables over one man. Dreyfus was brought back for a second trial and, astonishingly, convicted again. Then he was pardoned, and only years later fully cleared and returned to the army. Why does this belong in a Jewish story? Because the case showed that hatred of Jews had not disappeared in a modern, enlightened country; it could stand in a crowd in the capital. A young journalist from Vienna was in Paris covering the case. His name is tomorrow's lesson. And the Torah has a line for anyone who, like Zola, risks something to stop an injustice: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word is said twice. Some teachers read the doubling as a call to pursue justice by just means, too.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small unfairness near you: a rumor about someone, a person always blamed, a joke that lands on the same group every time. Don't solve it yet; just look at it straight, the way Zola looked at the papers and said, this is wrong. Then let one small way of refusing to go along take shape: a word, a question, a quiet no.
Dreyfus. A Jewish officer in France, falsely convicted of treason, defended by Zola's J'accuse, and in the end cleared. Today's word.
Your line: j'accuse. Two words on a front page, and a writer who paid for them. Day nine hundred ninety-nine, done.

1000.title: Herzl
1000.hook: Theodor Herzl calls the first Zionist Congress
1000.howItsDone: Herzl is remembered in Israel and in Zionist movements as a founder of political Zionism, and his motto, im tirtzu, if you will it, is often quoted; other Jews, then and now, disagreed with his vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dreyfus, and your line: j'accuse. Today, the journalist who was watching in Paris. And a small note: you've come one thousand days up this hill.

A man in a black beard and a formal coat stands at the front of a hall in Basel, Switzerland. In the seats are Jews from many countries: rabbis and students, doctors and businessmen, people who had never been in one room before. Many came in formal black coats, because he asked them to; he wanted the world to see that this was serious. He wrote plays, and he wrote for a Vienna newspaper. Now he was trying to win his people a state, starting with a meeting. His name is Theodor Herzl.
screen: `A HALL IN BASEL.` → `JEWS FROM MANY COUNTRIES.` → `A NATION STARTED WITH A MEETING.`

segments.voice: Herzl had not grown up dreaming of Zion. He was an assimilated Jew in Vienna, writing plays and reporting for a newspaper. What changed him, by his own telling, was what he saw of hatred against Jews, in Vienna and in France. Even Jews who did everything they were asked were not safe. So he wrote a short book called The Jewish State. Its argument was blunt: the hatred would not go away on its own, so Jews needed a homeland of their own, recognized by the nations, and should go about it in the open, with diplomacy, money and organization. Then he did the organizing himself. He called the Zionist Congress in Basel, sought meetings with rulers and their ministers, and wrote letters without end. He also wrote a novel about the future land, with a motto on its first page. In Hebrew it is known as im tirtzu: if you will it, it is no fairy tale. It is a dreamer's line, and also a planner's line. The psalm about the return to Zion says, "We were like unto them that dream." Herzl's line agrees it's a dream, then insists that wanting it, and working for it, can make it real. Herzl did not live to see a state. And not every Jew agreed with him, not by a long way. Tomorrow you'll meet the many kinds of Zionism, and the Jews who opposed all of them. Today, watch one man turn a longing into an agenda.
screen: `A VIENNA JOURNALIST CHANGES.` · `THE JEWISH STATE.` · `A CONGRESS IN BASEL.` · `A DREAM AND A PLAN.` · then, large: `IF YOU WILL IT, IT IS NO FAIRY TALE.`

segments.voice: Let one hope come up that you've long filed under someday: a garden, a language, a call you've been meaning to make. Hold it for a moment as a dream, then ask the planner's question: what is the very first step? Let the answer be small enough to be real.
Herzl. Theodor Herzl, the Vienna journalist who wrote The Jewish State and called the Zionist Congress in Basel. Today's word.
Your line: if you will it. A dream and a plan can live in the same sentence. A thousand days now, one at a time.

1001.title: Many Zionisms
1001.hook: political, religious, cultural and labor Zionism, and Jews who opposed it
1001.howItsDone: Jews today hold a wide range of views on Zionism and the State of Israel, from religious and secular Zionists to Jews who oppose Zionism on religious or political grounds, and the debate is part of Jewish communal life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herzl, and your line: if you will it. Today closes the week, and opens the argument his congress started.

Line up this week's stops. Jews everywhere, on every continent. Henrietta Szold, teaching newcomers. A line at the end of the seder that faces one city. Pogroms in the Russian Empire. A broken sword in Paris. A congress in Basel. By now it can sound as if everyone agreed on one answer. They didn't. Seat the Jews of that time around one table and you would hear plan after plan, and some people at the table saying the whole idea was a mistake.
screen: `A WEEK OF ROADS.` → `ONE TABLE, MANY PLANS.` → `AND SOME SAID NO.`

segments.voice: Zionism, the movement for a Jewish home in the land of Israel, was never one thing. Political Zionists, like Herzl, wanted a charter first: recognition from the great powers, then settlement. Others said, don't wait for permission, go and plant. Cultural Zionists, led by a writer who called himself Ahad Ha'am, one of the people, wanted something smaller and deeper: a center for Hebrew culture that would renew Jewish life everywhere. He also warned his readers that the land was not empty, that Arab villages and farmers were already there. Labor Zionists said renewal would come through work with the hands, farming and building together. Religious Zionists, in a movement called Mizrachi, joined as observant Jews, and some of them saw God's hand in it. And there were Jews who said no. Some Orthodox rabbis taught that the return would come with the Messiah, in God's time, and pointed to a passage in the Talmud about oaths not to force the end. Some Reform leaders said Judaism was a faith, not a nation, and their home was the country they lived in. Jewish socialists in Eastern Europe said: stay, and fight for rights right here. These arguments have not ended; Jews still hold all kinds of views. The Talmud tells of a voice from heaven about two schools that disagreed: these and these are the words of the living God. The law still followed one school, but both were kept. The tradition is used to a table full of argument.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one question where you hold a strong view, and picture someone you respect who sees it differently. Without arguing back, try saying their view in your head the way they would say it, at its best, and notice what they care about that you care about too. You don't have to change your mind; just let the other voice finish its sentence.
Many Zionisms. Political, practical, cultural, labor and religious, each with its own plan, and beside them, Jews who opposed the idea. Today's word.
